About the Author

   
About the Author

SONG YU-JEONG

was born in Ansan, Korea, and grew up in the nearby city of Suwon. Her debut novel The Memory Bookshop became a sensation in Korea after captivating readers online. Popular demand on the crowdfunding platform Tumblbug led to the book being self-published, before it was picked up by Dasan Books. The novel has since been translated into fourteen languages and is being published around the world. Song Yu-jeong moved back to her birthplace, Ansan, where she now spends her time writing.

SHANNA TAN

is a literary translator working from Korean, Chinese and Japanese into English. Her translations include the bestselling Welcome to the Hyunam-dong Bookshop by Hwang Bo-reum. Born and raised in Singapore, she is currently spending some time in Bangkok.

The Forever Night

The Forever Night

That day, the doctor asked, ‘What brings you here?’

I answered with a half-truth.

‘I’m constantly feeling breathless and anxious, but I have no idea why.’

How did I even end up at that clinic? Aside from being nowhere near my neighbourhood or the city centre, the clinic didn’t come with glowing reviews. If I cast my mind back, I could only say it happened to be a weekend and I was desperate for immediate help – or rather, medicine – to ease my desperation.

The place I found on the internet was in an old building tucked into a quiet market street, fifteen kilometres away by car. As usual, the GPS led me not to the car park, but the main entrance. Conjuring the image of the hanja character for endurance , I reminded myself to stay calm. After three futile rounds driving past the entrance, I concluded that the building didn’t have a car park after all, and I ended up at a public parking lot on a nearby street.

Up close, the building was even shabbier than I imagined. Cracked beige tiles plastered the walls, several were missing, and the signboards were draped in a thick layer of dust. To the left of the main entrance was a junkyard masquerading as a shop and on the other side was a stationery shop that made me nostalgic for my elementary school days, twenty years back. Displayed in the shopfront were gaudy red piggy banks printed with the  character for good luck and fortune.

Passing through the cavernous entrance, I was hit with an odour reminiscent of a dingy basement. After casting several back-and-forth glances at the stairs and the lift, I jabbed the clear plastic button. An orange glow appeared behind the upward-pointing silver triangle, yet another throwback to my nineties childhood.

Several moments later, the lift door opened with a mechanical clang. I was flustered. But that wasn’t all. Inside the lift, where one would expect to see a mirror or wall, was another door. Claustrophobia reared its head, and my eyes naturally darted to the stairs behind me. The old lift looked like it’d break down at any moment. I released my finger on the button and, with a rumble, the lift door clamped shut once more.

I turned towards the staircase. There wasn’t a single sign marking the levels. From somewhere above me, a draught blew in. I brought my sweaty palm to the nape of my neck and traced the goosebumps. You’re in the middle of the city, I chided myself. What can happen?

The clinic, it transpired, was on the third floor. Was there a law of sorts dictating that clinics be on the third floor? Random thoughts filled my mind as I climbed up. When I reached the landing, I came face to face with an opaque glass door that had become clouded over the years. I stuck my face close, but it was impossible to peer through. A green sticker slapped across the glass door read: HANMAEUM CLINIC. One Heart Clinic.

Should I turn back?

Doubt filled my mind, but I’d already come all this way. Gingerly, I elbowed the door open. Because of the thick draught stopper at the bottom, the glass door swung inwards with an uncomfortable squeak as a clear chime sounded above.

I took in the sight before me. Had I stepped into a time machine that had returned me to the past? Specks of dust hung unnaturally in mid-air as if time had stopped. What pulled me back to reality was the middle-aged nurse sitting at the reception counter opposite the entrance. I cast an anxious look at my hands and fiddled with my sleeves. I knew it was ridiculous, but I needed assurance that I hadn’t been sucked back into the nineties. Of course, in the space too cramped to be called a waiting area, the calendar on the counter confirmed that I was still in 2023.

‘Do you have an appointment?’

‘No, it’s my first time here.’

‘Alright. Please fill in this form.’ The nurse in a light yellow cardigan gestured at the countertop without sparing me a glance. ‘There’re a couple of patients ahead of you. Take a seat and I’ll call your name.’

Thinking that her appropriately bored tone perfectly fit the drab-looking place, I shuffled awkwardly to the long sofa. Sitting on one end was an elderly man with a walking stick, and an appropriate distance away in the middle was a mother-daughter pair who had their backs to each other. Everything about this place was perfectly appropriate, even the silence that hung in the air instead of the new-age music one would expect to hear.
